title: RAG is dead, right?? — Kuba Rogut, Turbopuffer

summary:
Kuba Rogut opens by acknowledging the Twitter discourse declaring RAG dead, then immediately undercuts it with Google search volume data showing RAG interest plateauing in 2024 before surging to a new inflection point mid-2025. He attributes the discourse to a narrow definition of RAG as a single vector search call, arguing that retrieval-augmented generation properly includes vector search, full-text search (BM25), grepping, globbing, regex, and filters. He defines agentic search not as simple file-system grep (as in Claude Code) but as giving agents tools to progressively and iteratively find and reason over context until they reach a satisfactory state.

Rogut presents Cursor as an exemplary agentic search implementation. Cursor indexes codebases upfront using Merkle trees to avoid re-embedding similar codebases across team members, storing results in Turbopuffer. Cursor's blog posts report a 24% increase in answer accuracy on their composer model, roughly 12.5–13.5% average across models, 2.6% better code retention in large codebases, and a 2.2% drop in dissatisfied user requests. Rogut notes these numbers seem small only because semantic search does not fire on every query.

He then contrasts Claude Code, which greps per session with no index and repeats discovery costs every run, against Cursor, which pays a one-time indexing cost for lightweight runtime tool calls. He frames embeddings as cached compute, where the decision to cache depends on query volume. He closes with Jeff Dean's principle that large context windows alone are insufficient; stage retrieval is needed to narrow trillions of tokens to the right million, which Turbopuffer sees as central to their customers' needs.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Turbopuffer Overview
sections.summary: Kuba Rogut introduces himself as a deploy engineer at Turbopuffer, a full-text and vector search database built from first principles on object storage, and announces the talk's theme: RAG is dead, and hybrid tool-rich retrieval is becoming the default for agentic search.

sections.title: RAG is Dead Discourse vs. Google Search Volume
sections.summary: Rogut references Twitter/X posts declaring RAG dead and agentic file search sufficient, then presents Google search volume data showing RAG interest surging to a new inflection point mid-2025, contradicting the discourse.

sections.title: Defining RAG vs. Agentic Search
sections.summary: Rogut argues RAG is narrowly misdefined as just vector search; proper retrieval includes vector search, full-text search (BM25), grep, glob, regex, and filters. Agentic search is not just file-system grep like Claude Code but giving agents tools to progressively and iteratively find and reason over context until satisfied.

sections.title: Cursor's Indexing Approach with Merkle Trees
sections.summary: Cursor, an early Turbopuffer customer, indexes codebases upfront by parsing, chunking, and embedding code. They use Merkle trees to detect similarity between codebases opened by team members, copying data and only re-embedding changed files, stored securely in Turbopuffer.

sections.title: Cursor's Semantic Search Metrics
sections.summary: Cursor's blog posts report a ~24% increase in answer accuracy on their composer model, ~12.5–13.5% average across models, 2.6% better code retention in large codebases, and 2.2% fewer dissatisfied user requests. These numbers appear small because semantic search does not fire on every query.

sections.title: Claude Code vs. Cursor: Per-Session Grep vs. Indexed Retrieval
sections.summary: Claude Code does not use vector search (per Boris Cherney), grepping per session and repeating discovery costs every run. Cursor pays a one-time indexing cost for lightweight runtime tool calls, saving tokens, time, and money. Rogut notes Turbopuffer team members switching from Claude Code to Cursor for speed.

sections.title: Embeddings as Cached Compute
sections.summary: Rogut frames embeddings and semantic search as cached compute, using the Claude Code vs. Cursor trace comparison to illustrate: repeated per-session grep costs tokens each time, while upfront indexing amortizes cost across all future queries.

sections.title: From Simple RAG to Agentic Retrieval
sections.summary: Sophisticated customers have moved beyond one-shot vector search into agentic retrieval: agents make many iterative calls, reason through multiple steps, search semantically or via full-text as needed, and fetch only what is required. Retrieval is no longer a single call but an iterative search-to-understand loop.

sections.title: Jeff Dean on Stage Retrieval and Context Windows
sections.summary: Rogut closes with Jeff Dean's principle: even with trillion-token context windows, you need stage retrieval—a lightweight mechanism to narrow down to the right million tokens. Turbopuffer customers embed trillions of tokens, and the key is retrieving the right subset for the context window.
